title: Australian Sports Anti-Doping Authority Amendment Bill 2013

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would strengthen the Australian Sports Anti-Doping Authority's (ASADA) investigation powers, expand information sharing and change how possible doping violations are handled.
ASADA's chief executive officer could compel people reasonably believed to hold relevant material to attend interviews, answer questions, provide information and produce documents or other things.
Notices could reach people beyond athletes and their support personnel, while Australia Post information sharing would exclude intercepting mail or examining its contents.
changes: Failing to meet a disclosure notice's requirements would carry a specified civil penalty of 30 penalty units.

Compelled material would be protected from use against its provider in criminal cases, except false or misleading information or document offences, and civil cases unrelated to the anti-doping legislation.
ASADA could keep documents and things supplied under notices for as long as necessary, and copy documents.
The existing eight-year deadline for starting anti-doping action would take priority over inconsistent state or territory laws.
The Anti-Doping Rule Violation Panel would stop recommending consequences to sporting tribunals and instead make findings about possible violations.
summary.affected: Athletes, athlete support personnel, other people holding relevant information, ASADA, Australia Post and the Anti-Doping Rule Violation Panel are affected.

speeches.speaker: Jacinta Collins
speeches.brief: The Australian Sports Anti-Doping Authority Amendment Bill 2013 was introduced to strengthen anti-doping powers, including compelling interviews and document production under civil penalty, and to implement recommendations from the Wood Review of Cycling Australia.

speeches.speaker: Gary Humphries
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the Australian Sports Anti-Doping Authority Amendment Bill 2013 was being rushed through the Senate with only 35 minutes for debate, which was an "absolute disgrace" given its controversial nature and significant impact on Australian sport. The speaker supported the bill's amendments but expressed ongoing concerns about balancing ASADA's new coercive powers with individual legal rights, and called for the government to quickly resolve the "dark cloud" over Australian sport by concluding investigations.
